## Solution

We work with the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $M = \langle x, y \rangle / \langle 2x - 3y \rangle$. Since $\langle x, y \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$ (free abelian of rank 2) and the relation submodule $N = \langle 2x - 3y \rangle$ is the cyclic submodule generated by the single relation vector $v = (2, -3) \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, we have

$$M \cong \mathbb{Z}^2 / \mathbb{Z}\cdot(2, -3).$$

**Smith Normal Form.** The presentation matrix is the $1 \times 2$ matrix
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \end{pmatrix}.$$

To compute the Smith normal form, we perform unimodular row and column operations. The greatest common divisor of the entries is $\gcd(2, 3) = 1$. Concretely, we use the Bézout identity $1 = (-1)\cdot 2 + (-1)\cdot(-3)$, i.e., $1 = -2 + 3$. Applying column operations:

- Add column 1 to column 2: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$.
- Add $2 \times$ column 2 to column 1: $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$.
- Negate column 2: $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
- Swap columns: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.

All operations are unimodular (determinant $\pm 1$), so the Smith normal form of $A$ is
$$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$

**Interpretation.** The single invariant factor is $d_1 = 1$. Since $d_1 = 1$, the torsion part is trivial (the quotient $\mathbb{Z}/1\mathbb{Z} = 0$). The remaining free part has rank $2 - 1 = 1$.

Equivalently, the vector $(2, -3)$ is **primitive** (its entries have gcd 1), so it can be extended to a basis of $\mathbb{Z}^2$. Explicitly, the matrix
$$P = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -3 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det(P) = 2\cdot(-1) - 1\cdot(-3) = -2 + 3 = 1$$
is unimodular, so its columns $\{(2,-3),\, (1,-1)\}$ form a basis of $\mathbb{Z}^2$. In this basis, the quotient by the first basis vector gives

$$M \cong \mathbb{Z}^2 / \mathbb{Z}\cdot(2,-3) \cong \mathbb{Z}\cdot(1,-1) \cong \mathbb{Z}.$$

**Conclusion.** The module $M$ is free of rank 1 with no torsion. Its invariant factor decomposition is

$$\boxed{M \cong \mathbb{Z}}.$$

The invariant factor list is $(1)$, which contributes no torsion, leaving a single free copy of $\mathbb{Z}$.
